passages.title: News of broken walls
passages.summary: Nehemiah serves in the Persian fortress of Susa. His brother Hanani arrives with men from Judah. They report that the survivors are in great trouble. Jerusalem’s wall is broken, and its gates are burned. Nehemiah sits down and weeps, fasts, and prays for days. He confesses the sins of Israel, his family, and himself. He recalls God’s promise to gather those who return to him. He asks for favor before the king, whose cupbearer he is.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson studies Nehemiah’s prayer about Jerusalem. What does he ask before he speaks to the king?

contextNote.title: A public need begins within royal service
contextNote.text: The prayer in verses 5–11 comes before any plan is spoken. Nehemiah includes himself in the confession (verse 6). He rests his request on a promise given through Moses (verses 8–9). In verse 11 he calls the king of Persia “this man.” Only the last line reveals his post. A cupbearer stands near the king every day. His position at court is where the answer will begin.

passages.title: Permission to rebuild
passages.summary: Four months later Nehemiah serves wine to the king with a sad face. The king asks why, and Nehemiah is very afraid. He says his fathers’ city lies in ruins. He prays quickly and asks to be sent to rebuild it. He asks for letters to governors and for timber from the king’s forest. The king grants it and sends officers with him. In Jerusalem he inspects the walls by night. He tells the leaders, and they agree to build despite mockery.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Nehemiah’s answer to mockery. What preparations support his call to rebuild?

contextNote.title: A wall requires permission and resources
contextNote.text: Between the king’s question and his own answer Nehemiah prays (verse 4). Then he names a time, letters for safe travel, and timber (verses 6–8). A bulla of the Persian period shows how letters were sealed. Verse 8 lists three uses for the wood. Safe travel and building materials depend on the king’s support. Nehemiah credits “the good hand of my God.” He also inspects the walls himself before he speaks to anyone (verses 12–16).

passages.title: Neighbors repair the walls
passages.summary: The high priest and his fellow priests rebuild the Sheep Gate. The chapter then moves around the wall section by section. Each group is named with the part it repairs. Goldsmiths, perfume makers, and merchants work beside district rulers. One ruler repairs his section with his daughters. Many people repair the wall opposite their own houses. The men of Tekoa repair two sections. Their nobles, however, refuse to work.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects the repairs with serving God. How do named families share the work?

contextNote.title: A work list also records unequal participation
contextNote.text: The list honors people by name, trade, and place. Verse 8 puts goldsmiths and perfume makers on the wall. Verse 12 names a ruler’s daughters among the builders. Many repair the stretch beside their own homes (verses 10, 23, 28–30). Verse 5 records the one refusal. The nobles of Tekoa would not bend their necks to the work. The ordinary men of Tekoa take a second section in verse 27.

passages.title: Builders keep watch
passages.summary: Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders and their wall. Nehemiah prays, and the wall rises to half its height. The enemies plot to attack Jerusalem. The people pray and post a guard day and night. Workers grow tired, and neighbors warn of raids ten times. Nehemiah stations families with swords, spears, and bows. Half his men work while half hold weapons. A trumpeter stays beside him, and they work from dawn until the stars appear.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies prayer and work during threats. How do guards and the trumpet help protect workers?

contextNote.title: A long wall creates a communication problem
contextNote.text: Verse 19 states the problem. The wall is long, and the workers are far apart. An attack on one section could succeed before others knew. Verse 20 gives the answer: one trumpet and one rallying point. The same verse says, “Our God will fight for us.” Trust and planning stand in one sentence, as in verse 9. Verse 14 names what the people defend: families and homes.

passages.title: Families lose land and freedom
passages.summary: A great outcry rises from the people and their wives against fellow Jews. Some have pledged fields and houses to buy grain in the famine. Some have borrowed to pay the king’s tax. Their children are being sold as servants. Nehemiah is very angry and accuses the nobles of charging interest. He says the community has been buying back Jews sold abroad. The nobles are silent and then promise to restore everything. As governor Nehemiah refuses the food allowance and feeds many at his own cost.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: What would stopping these charges change for the families?

contextNote.title: A shared building project does not remove inequality
contextNote.text: The enemy in this chapter is inside the walls. Verse 1 notes that wives join the outcry. Their argument in verse 5 is shared family: the same flesh, the same children. Yet their daughters are already in bondage, and the fields belong to others. Deuteronomy 23:19–20 forbids charging interest to a fellow Israelite. In verse 10 Nehemiah admits that he and his men have also lent. He ends the practice and gives up his own allowance (verses 14–18).

passages.title: Letters, threats, and a finished wall
passages.summary: The wall is nearly finished, with only the gate doors missing. Sanballat and Geshem invite Nehemiah to a meeting four times, meaning harm. He answers that he is doing a great work and cannot come down. A fifth letter accuses him of planning to be king. A hired prophet urges him to hide inside the temple. Nehemiah refuses and sees the plot. The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and the enemies lose heart. Yet Judah’s nobles keep exchanging letters with Tobiah.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Nehemiah’s response to attempts to stop him. Why does he refuse the proposed meetings?

contextNote.title: A completed wall cannot stop internal influence
contextNote.text: Verse 15 reports the finished wall. Verse 17 begins “Moreover” and turns to a problem stone cannot fix. Nobles of Judah trade letters with Tobiah. Verse 18 explains that many are bound to him by oath and marriage. They praise him to Nehemiah and carry Nehemiah’s words back (verse 19). Loyalties pass through the gates in both directions. In 13:4–5 Tobiah will be given a room in the temple.

passages.title: Guards and the return register
passages.summary: The wall is built, and the doors are hung. Nehemiah puts his brother Hanani and a trusted commander over Jerusalem. The gates are to stay shut until the sun is hot. Residents stand guard, each near his own house. The city is wide, but few people live in it. God moves Nehemiah to register the people by families. He finds the record of those who first returned. The list of families, numbers, and gifts follows.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: Why do the guards need clear instructions after the wall is built?

contextNote.title: Walls do not create a populated city
contextNote.text: Verse 4 describes a finished wall around a nearly empty city. The houses have not been rebuilt. A wall protects a people, and the people are missing. So the next task is to learn who belongs (verse 5). The old list in verses 6–73 matches Ezra 2. It ties the present community to the first return. Chapter 11 will use lots to move families into the city.

passages.title: Ezra reads and teachers explain
passages.summary: In the seventh month all the people gather at the Water Gate. They ask Ezra to bring the book of the law of Moses. He reads from early morning until noon on a wooden platform. Men, women, and all who can understand listen. Levites explain the reading, and the people weep. The leaders tell them not to grieve, since the day is holy. On the second day they read about the Feast of Booths. They build shelters of branches and keep the feast with great joy.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies help with understanding scripture. What do the teachers do after Ezra reads?

contextNote.title: Public reading requires understanding
contextNote.text: The people themselves ask for the book (verse 1). Verse 2 names the audience as men, women, and all who could understand. Verse 7 names thirteen Levites who helped them. Verse 8 gives their method: read clearly and give the sense. The goal is that the people understand what is read. Verse 12 traces the day’s joy to that understanding. On the next day they act on what they find (verses 14–16).

passages.title: A prayer remembers mercy and failure
passages.summary: On the twenty-fourth day the people fast in sackcloth. They read the law for a quarter of the day and confess for another quarter. The Levites lead a long prayer. It recalls creation, Abraham, Egypt, the sea, Sinai, and the manna. It admits that the fathers rebelled again and again. Each time God was merciful and did not abandon them. The prayer says God has been just and the people have done wrong. They are servants in their own land, so they make a written agreement.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: The people recall mercy during repeated failure. How does this shape their new promises?

contextNote.title: A prayer of rescue ends with continued dependence
contextNote.text: The prayer tells Israel’s history as mercy answered by rebellion. It does not end with a triumph. Verse 36 says the people are servants in the land given to their fathers. Verse 37 adds that its rich yield goes to foreign kings. The return has not ended their dependence. Verse 33 refuses to blame God for this. Out of that honest account they write and seal an agreement (verse 38).

passages.title: Promises to support worship
passages.summary: The agreement is sealed by Nehemiah, the priests, the Levites, and the leaders. The rest of the people join with an oath. They will not marry their children to the peoples of the land. They will not buy on the Sabbath, and they will cancel debts every seventh year. Each will pay a yearly sum for the temple’s service. They cast lots for bringing wood to the altar. They promise firstfruits and tithes for the priests and Levites. They say they will not neglect the house of their God.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: The Seminary overview studies promises about marriage and Sabbath rest. What supplies do the families also promise?

contextNote.title: A promise must supply recurring needs
contextNote.text: The written agreement names wood, produce, money, and the workers who need support. Verse 1 lists those who sealed it; a bulla is a seal’s impression. Temple service cannot continue through one large celebration alone. The promise turns shared identity into repeated duties. Verse 39 ends with a pledge not to neglect God’s house. Chapter 13:10–11 uses nearly the same words for a failure. Its later failures test whether those duties survive ordinary life.

passages.title: Families move into Jerusalem
passages.summary: The leaders live in Jerusalem. The other people cast lots to bring one family in ten into the city. The other nine stay in their towns. The people bless those who volunteer to move. The chapter lists the families of Judah and Benjamin who settle there. It lists priests, Levites, gatekeepers, and singers. An official at the king’s side handles the people’s affairs. The villages of Judah and Benjamin are named last.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: Who keeps daily temple service possible while families settle in different towns?

contextNote.title: Restoration changes where households live
contextNote.text: Chapter 7:4 said the city was large and nearly empty. Verse 1 fills it by lot, one family in ten. Verse 2 adds those who offered themselves freely. The people bless them, which shows the move was costly. A family left its fields and village for a city still in ruins. The lists that follow count the temple workers by name and number (verses 10–19). The city needs residents before it can serve as a center.

passages.title: Singers celebrate the rebuilt walls
passages.summary: The chapter lists the priests and Levites from the first return onward. For the wall’s dedication the Levites and singers are gathered from their villages. Priests and Levites purify themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall. Two large choirs walk along the top of the wall in opposite directions. Ezra leads one, and Nehemiah follows the other. They meet at the temple and sing loudly. The people offer great sacrifices and rejoice. Men are appointed that day over the storerooms for offerings.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: How do the women and children join the public thanks?

contextNote.title: A public celebration rests on maintained labor
contextNote.text: Tobiah had said a fox could break this wall (4:3). Now two choirs walk along its top (verses 31 and 38). Verse 43 says God gave the joy. It names women and children among those who rejoiced. The sound was heard far away. In Ezra 3:13 a mixed sound of joy and weeping carried far. Verses 44–47 arrange the workers’ daily portions on the same day.

passages.title: Nehemiah returns and changes the rules
passages.summary: The law is read, and the people separate from foreigners. Nehemiah has been away at the king’s court. On his return he finds Tobiah in a temple storeroom and throws him out. The Levites have not been paid and have gone back to their fields. Traders are selling on the Sabbath, so he shuts the gates. Jews have married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. He rebukes them harshly and drives out a priest’s son. He ends by asking God to remember him for good.
passages.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: The Seminary overview emphasizes Sabbath rest and keeping promises to God. How do Nehemiah’s actions affect workers and families?

contextNote.title: Reform reveals what earlier promises failed to sustain
contextNote.text: The people promised in 10:39 not to neglect God’s house. Verse 10 shows that promise broken. The Levites’ portions have stopped, so they have left to farm. The room meant for their supplies went to Tobiah (verse 5). Nehemiah’s repair is practical: honest treasurers to hand out shares (verse 13). Support, Sabbath, and marriage were the three pledges of chapter 10. All three have failed here, and the book ends with a prayer.

events.detail: The prayer tells Israel’s history as mercy answered by rebellion. It does not end with a triumph. Verse 36 says the people are servants in the land given to their fathers. Verse 37 adds that its rich yield goes to foreign kings. The return has not ended their dependence. Verse 33 refuses to blame God for this. Out of that honest account they write and seal an agreement (verse 38).
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: The people recall mercy during repeated failure. How does this shape their new promises?

events.title: Promises to support worship
events.summary: The agreement is sealed by Nehemiah, the priests, the Levites, and the leaders. The rest of the people join with an oath. They will not marry their children to the peoples of the land. They will not buy on the Sabbath, and they will cancel debts every seventh year. Each will pay a yearly sum for the temple’s service. They cast lots for bringing wood to the altar. They promise firstfruits and tithes for the priests and Levites. They say they will not neglect the house of their God.
events.detail: The written agreement names wood, produce, money, and the workers who need support. Verse 1 lists those who sealed it; a bulla is a seal’s impression. Temple service cannot continue through one large celebration alone. The promise turns shared identity into repeated duties. Verse 39 ends with a pledge not to neglect God’s house. Chapter 13:10–11 uses nearly the same words for a failure. Its later failures test whether those duties survive ordinary life.
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: The Seminary overview studies promises about marriage and Sabbath rest. What supplies do the families also promise?

events.title: Families move into Jerusalem
events.summary: The leaders live in Jerusalem. The other people cast lots to bring one family in ten into the city. The other nine stay in their towns. The people bless those who volunteer to move. The chapter lists the families of Judah and Benjamin who settle there. It lists priests, Levites, gatekeepers, and singers. An official at the king’s side handles the people’s affairs. The villages of Judah and Benjamin are named last.
events.detail: Chapter 7:4 said the city was large and nearly empty. Verse 1 fills it by lot, one family in ten. Verse 2 adds those who offered themselves freely. The people bless them, which shows the move was costly. A family left its fields and village for a city still in ruins. The lists that follow count the temple workers by name and number (verses 10–19). The city needs residents before it can serve as a center.
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: Who keeps daily temple service possible while families settle in different towns?

events.title: Singers celebrate the rebuilt walls
events.summary: The chapter lists the priests and Levites from the first return onward. For the wall’s dedication the Levites and singers are gathered from their villages. Priests and Levites purify themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall. Two large choirs walk along the top of the wall in opposite directions. Ezra leads one, and Nehemiah follows the other. They meet at the temple and sing loudly. The people offer great sacrifices and rejoice. Men are appointed that day over the storerooms for offerings.
events.detail: Tobiah had said a fox could break this wall (4:3). Now two choirs walk along its top (verses 31 and 38). Verse 43 says God gave the joy. It names women and children among those who rejoiced. The sound was heard far away. In Ezra 3:13 a mixed sound of joy and weeping carried far. Verses 44–47 arrange the workers’ daily portions on the same day.
events.uncertainty: The points show named towns and regions. Jerusalem’s gates and wall parts are not placed on the map.

lds.text: How do the women and children join the public thanks?

events.title: Nehemiah returns and changes the rules
events.summary: The law is read, and the people separate from foreigners. Nehemiah has been away at the king’s court. On his return he finds Tobiah in a temple storeroom and throws him out. The Levites have not been paid and have gone back to their fields. Traders are selling on the Sabbath, so he shuts the gates. Jews have married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. He rebukes them harshly and drives out a priest’s son. He ends by asking God to remember him for good.
events.detail: The people promised in 10:39 not to neglect God’s house. Verse 10 shows that promise broken. The Levites’ portions have stopped, so they have left to farm. The room meant for their supplies went to Tobiah (verse 5). Nehemiah’s repair is practical: honest treasurers to hand out shares (verse 13). Support, Sabbath, and marriage were the three pledges of chapter 10. All three have failed here, and the book ends with a prayer.

guides.title: Nehemiah: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A wall requires permission and resources
steps.text: Between the king’s question and his own answer Nehemiah prays (verse 4). Then he names a time, letters for safe travel, and timber (verses 6–8). A bulla of the Persian period shows how letters were sealed. Verse 8 lists three uses for the wood. Safe travel and building materials depend on the king’s support. Nehemiah credits “the good hand of my God.” He also inspects the walls himself before he speaks to anyone (verses 12–16).

steps.title: A shared building project does not remove inequality
steps.text: The enemy in this chapter is inside the walls. Verse 1 notes that wives join the outcry. Their argument in verse 5 is shared family: the same flesh, the same children. Yet their daughters are already in bondage, and the fields belong to others. Deuteronomy 23:19–20 forbids charging interest to a fellow Israelite. In verse 10 Nehemiah admits that he and his men have also lent. He ends the practice and gives up his own allowance (verses 14–18).

steps.title: Public reading requires understanding
steps.text: The people themselves ask for the book (verse 1). Verse 2 names the audience as men, women, and all who could understand. Verse 7 names thirteen Levites who helped them. Verse 8 gives their method: read clearly and give the sense. The goal is that the people understand what is read. Verse 12 traces the day’s joy to that understanding. On the next day they act on what they find (verses 14–16).

chapterMaps.narrative: Nehemiah serves in the Persian fortress of Susa. His brother Hanani arrives with men from Judah. They report that the survivors are in great trouble. Jerusalem’s wall is broken, and its gates are burned. Nehemiah sits down and weeps, fasts, and prays for days. He confesses the sins of Israel, his family, and himself. He recalls God’s promise to gather those who return to him. He asks for favor before the king, whose cupbearer he is.

chapterMaps.narrative: Four months later Nehemiah serves wine to the king with a sad face. The king asks why, and Nehemiah is very afraid. He says his fathers’ city lies in ruins. He prays quickly and asks to be sent to rebuild it. He asks for letters to governors and for timber from the king’s forest. The king grants it and sends officers with him. In Jerusalem he inspects the walls by night. He tells the leaders, and they agree to build despite mockery.

chapterMaps.narrative: The high priest and his fellow priests rebuild the Sheep Gate. The chapter then moves around the wall section by section. Each group is named with the part it repairs. Goldsmiths, perfume makers, and merchants work beside district rulers. One ruler repairs his section with his daughters. Many people repair the wall opposite their own houses. The men of Tekoa repair two sections. Their nobles, however, refuse to work.

chapterMaps.narrative: Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders and their wall. Nehemiah prays, and the wall rises to half its height. The enemies plot to attack Jerusalem. The people pray and post a guard day and night. Workers grow tired, and neighbors warn of raids ten times. Nehemiah stations families with swords, spears, and bows. Half his men work while half hold weapons. A trumpeter stays beside him, and they work from dawn until the stars appear.

chapterMaps.narrative: A great outcry rises from the people and their wives against fellow Jews. Some have pledged fields and houses to buy grain in the famine. Some have borrowed to pay the king’s tax. Their children are being sold as servants. Nehemiah is very angry and accuses the nobles of charging interest. He says the community has been buying back Jews sold abroad. The nobles are silent and then promise to restore everything. As governor Nehemiah refuses the food allowance and feeds many at his own cost.

chapterMaps.narrative: The wall is nearly finished, with only the gate doors missing. Sanballat and Geshem invite Nehemiah to a meeting four times, meaning harm. He answers that he is doing a great work and cannot come down. A fifth letter accuses him of planning to be king. A hired prophet urges him to hide inside the temple. Nehemiah refuses and sees the plot. The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and the enemies lose heart. Yet Judah’s nobles keep exchanging letters with Tobiah.

chapterMaps.narrative: The wall is built, and the doors are hung. Nehemiah puts his brother Hanani and a trusted commander over Jerusalem. The gates are to stay shut until the sun is hot. Residents stand guard, each near his own house. The city is wide, but few people live in it. God moves Nehemiah to register the people by families. He finds the record of those who first returned. The list of families, numbers, and gifts follows.

chapterMaps.narrative: In the seventh month all the people gather at the Water Gate. They ask Ezra to bring the book of the law of Moses. He reads from early morning until noon on a wooden platform. Men, women, and all who can understand listen. Levites explain the reading, and the people weep. The leaders tell them not to grieve, since the day is holy. On the second day they read about the Feast of Booths. They build shelters of branches and keep the feast with great joy.

chapterMaps.narrative: On the twenty-fourth day the people fast in sackcloth. They read the law for a quarter of the day and confess for another quarter. The Levites lead a long prayer. It recalls creation, Abraham, Egypt, the sea, Sinai, and the manna. It admits that the fathers rebelled again and again. Each time God was merciful and did not abandon them. The prayer says God has been just and the people have done wrong. They are servants in their own land, so they make a written agreement.

They will not marry their children to the peoples of the land. They will not buy on the Sabbath, and they will cancel debts every seventh year. Each will pay a yearly sum for the temple’s service. They cast lots for bringing wood to the altar. They promise firstfruits and tithes for the priests and Levites. They say they will not neglect the house of their God.

chapterMaps.narrative: The chapter lists the priests and Levites from the first return onward. For the wall’s dedication the Levites and singers are gathered from their villages. Priests and Levites purify themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall. Two large choirs walk along the top of the wall in opposite directions. Ezra leads one, and Nehemiah follows the other. They meet at the temple and sing loudly. The people offer great sacrifices and rejoice. Men are appointed that day over the storerooms for offerings.

chapterMaps.narrative: The law is read, and the people separate from foreigners. Nehemiah has been away at the king’s court. On his return he finds Tobiah in a temple storeroom and throws him out. The Levites have not been paid and have gone back to their fields. Traders are selling on the Sabbath, so he shuts the gates. Jews have married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. He rebukes them harshly and drives out a priest’s son. He ends by asking God to remember him for good.
